newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH BANKERS CALL FOR PRICING OF EURO COSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH BANKERS CALL FOR PRICING OF EURO COSTS.

text.p: Banks' costs of the transition to a common European currency should be transparently priced, Finnish Bankers' Association officials said in a newsletter received on Wednesday.
"Costs should be transparent ... in the pricing of euro-related changes," managing director Matti Sipila said.
"The main goal will be that the transition should be economically reasonable," director Kaija Erjanti wrote in a separate article.
The shift to the euro would bring considerable costs to the banking sector and would tie up resources throughout the transition period, Erjanti said.
The association has estimated the direct costs of Finnish banks' transition to the common currency at 600-700 million markka.
Banks have also accepted the fact that shifting to the euro will mean losses of revenues from foreign-exchange operations, Sipila said.
While it would be possible for banks to create a full range of transition period services by 1999, that would mean increased operating expenses, Sipila said.

"I think it would be premature and, as far as the transition period is concerned, impossible that banks should offer an unlimited number of euro services during the transition period without pricing," Sipila said.
"The banks, of course, will decide independently on their readiness and pricing," he said.

Despite the uncertainty surrounding the timetable for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and Finnish membership of the bloc, banks would need to make big investments this year to prepare for the euro, he said.
During the 1999-2001 transition phase, the euro would only be used as an account currency, whereas bills and coins would be introduced by the beginning of 2002 at the latest, Erjanti said.
"The flexible solution jointly agreed by the banks will mean substational cost savings for other parties, especially the public sector and companies," Erjanti said.
During the transition period, banks would mainly operate in markka in their internal systems and would keep their clients accounts in markka up to about the end of 2001, she said.
A customer's "euro account" would in fact be a markka account with a euro-denominated bank statement, she said.
Interest on existing loans and deposits would not be affected by the shift to the euro, Erjanti said.
The expansion of national financial markets into a broad euro region market could bring changes in the ways reference interest rates are calculated, Erjanti said.
